questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
questions.title: Docker Image vs Container — Key Difference
questions.direct_answer: A Docker image is a read-only blueprint containing your application code, dependencies, and runtime — like a class definition in Java. A Docker container is a running instance of that image — like an object instantiated from a class. You can run multiple containers from the same image, each isolated from the others.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Docker's fundamental building blocks and the relationship between static artifacts and runtime instances
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking images and containers are the same thing, or believing you modify an image when you change a running container
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the class-object parallel clearly and mention that containers have their own writable layer on top of the read-only image layers

sections.title: Images as Blueprints, Containers as Running Instances
sections.content: Think of a **Docker image** as a packaged Spring Boot JAR file sitting on disk — it contains everything your app needs: compiled code, libraries, configuration files, even the Java runtime. The image itself doesn't run or do anything; it's a **read-only template**. A **Docker container** is what you get when you actually start that image — it's the live, running process with its own memory space, network interface, and filesystem. The key insight: one image can spawn dozens of containers, each running independently. This is exactly like how one Java class definition (the blueprint) can create many object instances at runtime. The image stays unchanged no matter how many containers you create from it, just like your class file doesn't change when you call **new Order()** a hundred times. When you package your Spring Boot app as a Docker image using a Dockerfile, you're creating that reusable blueprint. When you run **docker run myapp:latest**, you're instantiating a container from that blueprint.

sections.title: Image vs Container

rows: Stored on disk, can be shared

sections.title: When You Work With Each
sections.content: Use **docker build** to create or update an image when you've changed your Dockerfile or application code — this produces the blueprint. Use **docker push** to share that image with others via Docker Hub or a private registry. Use **docker pull** to download an image someone else built, like the official postgres:15 or openjdk:17 base images. Then use **docker run** to start a container from any local image — this is when your app actually executes. You'll use **docker stop** and **docker start** to pause and resume containers without losing their state, and **docker rm** to delete a container entirely. If you're debugging, you might use **docker exec** to run a shell inside a running container — that's interacting with the container, not the image. Remember: you build and distribute images, but you run and monitor containers.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Docker image**: read-only template containing app code, dependencies, and runtime — analogous to a Java class
**Docker container**: live running instance of an image with its own writable layer — analogous to a Java object
**One-to-many relationship**: one image can spawn unlimited containers, each isolated from the others
**Immutability**: changes inside a container don't affect the original image unless you commit them
**Build vs run**: docker build creates images, docker run creates containers from images
**Registry workflow**: images are pushed to and pulled from registries like Docker Hub; containers exist only on the host machine
**Layered architecture**: images are built from layers; containers add a thin writable layer on top at runtime

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A Docker image is a read-only blueprint that packages your application and everything it needs to run — it's like a class definition in Java. A Docker container is a running instance of that image, like an object you create from a class. So when you write a Dockerfile and run docker build, you're creating an image. When you run docker run on that image, you're starting a container. The same image can power dozens of containers at once, each completely isolated. For example, if I've got a Spring Boot app packaged as myapp:latest, that's my image. When I do docker run myapp:latest three times, I get three separate containers, each running the same code but with its own memory and filesystem. The image itself never changes when a container runs — it stays read-only. If a container crashes or I stop it, the image is still there ready to start another container. The key difference is state: images are static files on disk, containers are live processes. One common mistake is thinking you modify the image when you change files inside a container — you don't. You're only changing that container's writable layer. That's why I can confidently say images are the build artifact, containers are the runtime instances. In a Spring Boot context, the image holds your JAR and the JDK, but the container is what actually executes your application code and handles requests.

groups.heading: Docker image
groups.text: A read-only blueprint. It's built from a Dockerfile, stored on disk as stacked layers, and never modified after creation. Think of it as a Java class definition.

groups.heading: Docker container
groups.text: A running instance created from an image. It has an active process, a writable layer on top of the image, and its own network. Think of it as an object instantiated from that class.

beats.text: You push images to registries and version them. You run containers in your environments. Deploying a new version means building a new image and replacing the running containers — you never patch a live container.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: containers are ephemeral by default. Any files written inside a container disappear when the container is removed. If you need persistence, that's what Docker volumes are for.

questions.question: What are Docker image layers and how does layer caching work?
questions.title: Docker Image Layers and Layer Caching
questions.direct_answer: Docker images are built from layers — each instruction in your Dockerfile (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new read-only layer. Docker caches these layers by content hash, so if a layer hasn't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. This makes subsequent builds much faster.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of how Docker builds work and whether you've optimized real Dockerfiles for faster iteration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing Dockerfiles that copy all source code first, then install dependencies — this invalidates the cache on every code change and forces a full rebuild
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the optimization pattern: copy dependency files first (pom.xml or build.gradle), run dependency download, then copy source code — so the expensive dependency layer stays cached even when code changes

sections.title: Understanding Docker Image Layers and Build Caching
sections.content: Think of a Docker image as a **layered cake** where each layer is read-only and stacked on top of the previous one. When you build a Docker image, every instruction in your Dockerfile (like RUN, COPY, or ADD) creates a new layer. Docker is smart about this: it calculates a **hash** (fingerprint) of each layer based on the instruction and the files involved. If that exact layer was built before and nothing changed, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of rebuilding it from scratch. This is **layer caching**, and it's why your second build of the same Dockerfile is much faster than the first. The catch is that once a layer changes, all layers after it must be rebuilt — the cache is **invalidated** from that point down. This matters a lot for Spring Boot apps: if you copy your source code early in the Dockerfile, every code change forces Docker to rebuild the expensive dependency download step. But if you copy pom.xml first, run mvn dependency:go-offline, and only then copy source code, the dependency layer stays cached across code changes. Understanding this ordering is the difference between 10-second builds and 3-minute builds during development.

sections.title: Optimized Multi-Stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot with Layer Caching
sections.content:
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only dependency files first - this layer rarely changes
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline

# Now copy source code - changes frequently
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-jammy
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the built JAR from the build stage
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar

# Run as non-root user for security
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Layer**: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a read-only layer identified by a content hash — changing the instruction or its inputs creates a new layer
**Cache invalidation**: Once a layer changes, all subsequent layers must be rebuilt — order matters for build speed
**Dependency optimization**: Copy dependency descriptors (pom.xml, build.gradle) before source code so the expensive dependency download layer stays cached
**Multi-stage builds**: Use a build stage with full JDK and Maven, then copy only the JAR to a slim runtime stage with just JRE — reduces final image size by 60-70%
**Layer sharing**: Multiple images built from the same base image share those base layers on disk — pulling openjdk:17 once benefits all images using it
**Build context**: Docker sends your entire build context (the directory with Dockerfile) to the daemon — use .dockerignore to exclude target/, node_modules/, .git/ and speed up builds
**Intermediate containers**: Each layer is technically created by running a temporary container, executing the instruction, and committing the result — this is why RUN commands can fail during build

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say Docker images are built from layers, where each instruction in the Dockerfile creates a new read-only layer. Docker caches these layers based on a hash of the instruction and its inputs, so if nothing changed, it reuses the cached layer instead of rebuilding. This is why the second build is way faster. The key thing I learned when building Spring Boot images is that order matters a lot. If you copy all your source code early in the Dockerfile, then run Maven to download dependencies, every single code change invalidates the cache and forces a full dependency re-download. That's painful because Maven might pull 200MB of JARs every time. The optimization pattern is to copy just the pom.xml first, run Maven dependency download, and only then copy your source code. That way, the dependency layer stays cached as long as your pom.xml doesn't change. In my projects, this cut build times from 3 minutes down to 10 seconds during development. One thing to watch out for is the build context size. Docker sends your entire project directory to the daemon before building, so if you've got a huge target folder or node_modules, it slows everything down. Always use a dockerignore file to exclude build artifacts and version control directories. For production, I'd also mention multi-stage builds where you compile in one stage with the full JDK and Maven, then copy only the JAR to a second stage with just the JRE. That cuts the final image from maybe 700MB down to 250MB.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Every line in your Dockerfile creates a layer — and the order you write those lines determines whether your builds take 10 seconds or 5 minutes.

beats.text: Docker images are built as a stack of layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile — FROM, COPY, RUN — adds one immutable layer on top of the previous ones. The final image is all those layers combined.

Layer caching is the real payoff. If a layer's instruction and its inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. One changed layer invalidates all layers below it.

For Java, the optimization is to COPY pom.xml first and run Maven dependency download as a separate layer. That dependencies layer gets cached. Then COPY your source code. Now when you change a Java file, only the compile layer rebuilds — the multi-minute dependency download is skipped.
production trap: copying all source files in a single COPY instruction means any file change invalidates the dependency download layer, making every build slow. Split COPY into two steps.

speakable_v2.cap: Put the things that change least at the top of the Dockerfile, and the things that change most — your source code — at the bottom. Cache invalidation flows downward.

questions.question: What do 'docker ps' and 'docker images' show and how are they different?
questions.title: docker ps vs docker images — What They Show
questions.direct_answer: The docker images command lists all Docker images stored on your local machine — these are the blueprints. The docker ps command lists currently running containers — these are the live instances. Use docker ps -a to see all containers including stopped ones. They're different because images are static templates while containers are active processes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Docker CLI proficiency and understanding of the image-container distinction in practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two commands or not knowing that docker ps only shows running containers by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the key columns in docker ps output: CONTAINER ID for reference, IMAGE showing which blueprint was used, STATUS showing container state, and PORTS showing network mappings

sections.title: Two Commands for Two Different Artifact Types
sections.content: The **docker images** command shows you all the images stored locally on your machine — the read-only blueprints you've either built yourself or pulled from a registry. Think of it as listing all the JAR files you've compiled. The **docker ps** command shows running containers — the actual live processes executing right now. Think of it as listing all the Java processes currently running with their process IDs. By default, docker ps only shows running containers, but docker ps -a shows all containers including stopped ones. Why two commands? Because they manage fundamentally different things. An image sitting on disk doing nothing takes up storage but uses zero CPU or memory. A running container consumes system resources and has an active lifecycle. You might have 50 images on your machine but only 3 running containers. These commands let you inspect each layer: docker images for the build artifacts, docker ps for the runtime instances.

sections.title: docker images vs docker ps

rows: REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED, SIZE
CONTAINER ID, IMAGE, STATUS, PORTS, NAMES
Check what images you have available

sections.title: When You Run Each Command
sections.content: Run **docker images** when you want to see what application blueprints are available to run. This is useful before starting a container (to check if you need to pull an image first), after building a new image (to verify the build succeeded), or when cleaning up disk space (to find large unused images to remove with docker rmi). Run **docker ps** when you need to monitor what's actively running — for example, checking if your Spring Boot container started successfully, finding the container ID to attach logs or execute a shell, or verifying which ports are mapped. Use **docker ps -a** when debugging why a container stopped, finding stopped containers to restart with docker start, or cleaning up old containers with docker rm. In a typical workflow, you'd run docker images first to confirm myapp:latest exists, then docker run myapp:latest to start it, then docker ps to verify it's running and see which port it's bound to.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker images**: lists all Docker images on your local machine with REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED date, and SIZE
**docker ps**: lists currently running containers with CONTAINER ID, IMAGE source, COMMAND executed, STATUS, and exposed PORTS
**docker ps -a flag**: shows all containers including stopped ones, essential for debugging failed containers
**CONTAINER ID**: unique identifier for each container instance, used in docker stop, docker rm, docker logs commands
**IMAGE column in ps**: shows which image the container was created from, linking the runtime back to its blueprint
**STATUS field**: shows container state like Up 2 minutes or Exited (1) 5 seconds ago with exit code
**Cleanup distinction**: use docker rmi to remove images, docker rm to remove containers — they're separate cleanup operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The docker images command shows all the Docker images stored locally on your machine — these are the blueprints or templates. You'll see columns like REPOSITORY for the image name, TAG for the version, IMAGE ID as a unique identifier, and SIZE. So if I've built a Spring Boot app as myapp:latest, that shows up here. The docker ps command shows running containers — the actual live instances. You see different columns here: CONTAINER ID, which image it came from, the STATUS like Up 10 minutes, and PORTS showing network mappings. By default, docker ps only shows running containers. If I want to see stopped ones too, I use docker ps -a — the a flag means all. The key difference is that images are static files on disk, while containers are active processes. It's like the difference between listing JAR files in your target directory versus listing running Java processes with their PIDs. One common mistake is expecting docker ps to show images or docker images to show containers — they're completely separate. In practice, I use docker images to check what's available to run and to verify a build succeeded. I use docker ps to monitor what's currently running, find container IDs for debugging, and check if my app started successfully. For example, after running docker run myapp:latest, I'd immediately run docker ps to confirm it's up and see which host port got mapped to the container's port 8080.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Two of the most-used Docker commands show completely different things — and mixing them up tells an interviewer you haven't actually used Docker.

groups.heading: docker images
groups.text: Lists all images on your local machine — the read-only blueprints. Shows repository name, tag, image ID, creation date, and size. Images stay until you remove them with docker rmi.

groups.heading: docker ps
groups.text: Lists currently running containers. Shows container ID, which image it came from, the running command, uptime, status, exposed ports, and name. Stopped containers don't appear here.

items: docker ps: running containers only — add -a to see stopped containers too
docker images: all local images regardless of whether any containers are running
You can have an image with zero running containers, and that's normal

beats.text: After you run docker-compose down, docker ps shows nothing. But docker images still shows all your images — they're on disk, ready to run again.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: docker ps -a reveals stopped containers that are consuming disk space. Run docker system prune to clean up stopped containers, dangling images, and unused networks in one go.

questions.question: What does it mean that Docker containers are ephemeral, and how do you persist data?
questions.title: Docker Containers Are Ephemeral — Persisting Data
questions.direct_answer: Ephemeral means container filesystem changes are lost when the container is removed — any data you write inside the container disappears. To persist data across container restarts or share data between containers, use Docker volumes, which are managed storage areas that exist outside the container lifecycle and survive container deletion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of container lifecycle and data persistence strategies — critical for production apps with databases, file uploads, or logs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming data written inside a container (like uploaded files or database writes) is permanent, then losing application state or user data when the container restarts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between Docker volumes (managed by Docker in /var/lib/docker/volumes) and bind mounts (direct mapping to a host directory) — both persist data but volumes are portable across environments while bind mounts are good for development hot-reloading

sections.title: Container Ephemerality and Data Persistence Strategies
sections.content: **Ephemeral** means temporary or short-lived. When you run a Docker container, it gets its own filesystem layer on top of the image layers — this is a **writable layer** where all changes go. Write a log file, upload a profile picture, create a database record — they all live in this writable layer. The catch is that this layer is tightly coupled to the container's lifecycle: when you run docker rm to remove the container, the writable layer is deleted and all that data is gone forever. This is by design: containers are meant to be **disposable** and **replaceable**. You should be able to stop a container, delete it, spin up a new one from the same image, and have it work identically. But real applications need to persist data. If you're running PostgreSQL in a container, you can't lose the entire database every time you restart. If users upload profile photos to your Spring Boot app, those files need to survive deployments. Docker provides two main solutions: **volumes** (managed storage that Docker creates and maintains outside the container) and **bind mounts** (direct mapping to a specific directory on your host machine). Both let data outlive the container, but volumes are the recommended approach for production because they're portable, backed up easily, and managed by Docker commands.

sections.title: Spring Boot App with PostgreSQL Using Named Volume
sections.content:
// docker-compose.yml for a Spring Boot app with persistent database
version: '3.8'

services:
  app:
    image: myapp:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/myapp
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: postgres
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: secret
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # Named volume persists database
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

volumes:
  postgres-data:  # Docker creates and manages this volume

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Ephemeral filesystem**: The writable layer of a container is deleted when you run docker rm — any data written during the container's lifetime is lost
**Volumes**: Managed by Docker and stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes on Linux — they persist independently of containers and can be attached to multiple containers
**Bind mounts**: Map a host directory directly into the container — useful for development (hot-reload source code) but less portable across environments
**Named volumes**: Created with docker volume create or declared in docker-compose.yml — easier to manage and back up than anonymous volumes
**Volume drivers**: Docker supports plugins for network storage (NFS, AWS EFS, Azure Files) so volumes can be shared across multiple hosts in a cluster
**Database persistence**: Always mount the database data directory to a volume — for PostgreSQL it's /var/lib/postgresql/data, for MySQL it's /var/lib/mysql
**Stateless vs stateful**: Design your app to be stateless (no local file uploads, use S3 or object storage) — this makes scaling and container replacement trivial

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Ephemeral means the container's filesystem is temporary and disposable. When you run a container, Docker gives it a writable layer on top of the read-only image layers. Anything you write — log files, uploaded images, database records — goes into that writable layer. But here's the problem: when you remove the container with docker rm, that writable layer is deleted and all your data is gone. This is actually by design because containers are meant to be replaceable. You should be able to spin up a new container from the same image and have it work the same way. But in real applications, you obviously need to persist some data. If I'm running a Spring Boot app with PostgreSQL in a container, I can't lose the entire database every time I restart. The solution is Docker volumes. A volume is storage that Docker creates and manages outside the container lifecycle. You mount it into the container at a specific path, like /var/lib/postgresql/data for Postgres, and now all database writes go to the volume instead of the container's writable layer. When you delete the container, the volume stays intact with all your data. You can attach that same volume to a new container and pick up right where you left off. There's also bind mounts, which map a host directory directly into the container. I use bind mounts during development to hot-reload my Spring Boot source code without rebuilding the image. But for production, volumes are better because they're managed by Docker and work the same way whether you're on your laptop, a staging server, or AWS. One mistake I see is people uploading files inside the container and wondering why they disappear after a deployment. Always use volumes for persistent data or, even better, use object storage like S3 so your app stays completely stateless.

How do you back up data in a Docker volume?

speakable_v2.standard_example: MySQL container with a Docker volume for database persistence
speakable_v2.hook: Ephemeral sounds scary but it's actually a feature — until you run a database container without a volume and lose all your data on restart.

beats.text: Every container has a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image. Anything written inside the container — files, logs, database rows — goes into that writable layer. When you remove the container, that layer is deleted. That's what ephemeral means.

For stateless apps like a Spring Boot REST API, this is fine. The app doesn't write anything locally, so ephemeral containers work perfectly. For stateful workloads like a database, you need data to survive container restarts.

items: Docker volume: Docker-managed storage outside the container lifecycle — survives docker rm
Bind mount: maps a specific host directory into the container — useful for dev
Usage: docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/mysql mysql attaches a volume at the database data path

beats.text: gotcha: if you run a MySQL container in local dev without a volume and then run docker-compose down, you lose your entire local database. Always define volumes for stateful services in docker-compose.yml.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless containers love being ephemeral. Stateful containers need volumes. Knowing the difference is what separates a developer who understands Docker from one who just copies commands.

questions.question: What is the sequence of steps from pulling a Docker image to running a container?
questions.title: Docker Pull to Running Container — The Full Sequence
questions.direct_answer: First, docker pull downloads an image from a registry like Docker Hub to your local machine — this step is optional because docker run does it automatically if the image isn't found locally. Then docker run creates a new container from that image, sets up networking and volumes, and starts the container process. The full workflow is: pull image from registry, create container instance, start container process.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Docker's basic workflow and the relationship between registries, local images, and running containers — foundational knowledge for deployment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that docker run automatically pulls missing images, or thinking docker pull is always required before running a container
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that docker run is actually a convenience command that combines docker create (which sets up the container without starting it) and docker start (which launches the process) — understanding this split helps with debugging and advanced workflows

sections.title: Docker Image Pull and Container Launch Workflow
sections.content: The journey from an image sitting in a remote registry to a running container on your machine has three main phases, though you usually only see one command. First, there's the **registry** — a storage and distribution system for Docker images, with Docker Hub being the default public registry. When you reference an image like postgres:15 or mycompany/myapp:v2.1, Docker looks for it in the registry. The **docker pull** command downloads all the layers of that image to your local machine and stores them in Docker's image cache. Here's the clever part: you don't actually need to run docker pull explicitly. When you execute **docker run**, Docker first checks if the image exists locally, and if it doesn't, it automatically pulls it from the registry. This is why your first docker run postgres takes a while (downloading layers) but subsequent runs are instant (image is cached). Once the image is local, docker run creates a **container instance** — this allocates a writable layer on top of the read-only image layers, sets up networking (assigns an IP, connects to networks), mounts any volumes you specified, and configures environment variables. Finally, it starts the container's main process (whatever ENTRYPOINT or CMD was defined in the image). Understanding this flow helps you debug issues: if docker run fails immediately, the problem is usually in the create phase (bad port mapping, missing volume). If it starts but crashes, the issue is in your application code.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Container Launch with Explicit Commands
Key Points
content: **docker pull**: Downloads an image from a registry to your local image cache — optional because docker run does this automatically if the image is missing
**docker run**: Combines docker create and docker start — it's the most common command and handles the entire workflow from image to running container
**docker create**: Sets up a container instance with networking, volumes, and environment variables but doesn't start the process — useful for pre-configuring containers
**docker start**: Launches the main process of an already-created container — you use this to restart stopped containers without recreating them
**Image layers**: When pulling, Docker downloads only the layers you don't already have — if you pull postgres:15 and postgres:16, they share base layers and the second pull is faster
**Registry authentication**: Private registries require docker login before pulling — Docker Hub allows anonymous pulls for public images up to rate limits
**Container naming**: docker run --name myapp assigns a friendly name — without it Docker generates a random name like quirky_einstein, making management harder

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The sequence starts with the image in a registry, which is basically a storage system for Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry, but companies often use private registries like AWS ECR or Azure Container Registry. When you run docker pull followed by an image name, Docker downloads all the layers of that image to your local machine. But here's the thing: you don't actually need to run docker pull separately. When you do docker run, Docker first checks if the image exists locally. If it doesn't, it automatically pulls it from the registry. So docker pull is more of an optimization — you might run it ahead of time to pre-download images, but it's not required. Once the image is local, docker run creates a new container. This step sets up the container's configuration: it allocates a writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers, assigns an IP address and connects it to a network, mounts any volumes you specified, and sets environment variables. Then it starts the container's main process, whatever was defined in the ENTRYPOINT or CMD instruction of the Dockerfile. Most people only use docker run because it does everything in one command. But docker run is actually a convenience wrapper around two separate commands: docker create and docker start. Create sets up the container without starting it, and start launches the process. This split is useful when you're debugging or doing advanced stuff like pre-creating a bunch of containers with different configs and then starting them all at once. I remember being confused about why my first docker run postgres took 2 minutes but the second one was instant. It's because the first time, Docker was pulling all the layers from Docker Hub. The second time, the image was already in my local cache, so it just created and started the container immediately.

speakable_v2.hook: Most people jump straight to docker run — but knowing what actually happens under the hood shows you understand Docker, not just its commands.

items: docker pull: fetches the image from a registry to your local cache
docker run: creates a container from the image and starts it immediately
If the image isn't local, docker run pulls it automatically first
Internally, docker run = docker create + docker start in one step

beats.text: When you first run docker run eclipse-temurin:21 on a fresh machine, Docker checks local cache, finds nothing, pulls the image layers from Docker Hub, then starts the container. Next time it uses the cached image and starts in seconds.

Stopping and cleanup: docker stop sends SIGTERM to the main process for graceful shutdown. After a timeout it sends SIGKILL. Docker rm removes the stopped container. Docker rmi removes the image from local storage.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: a stopped container still exists and takes up disk space. Use docker ps -a to see it, and docker system prune to clean up all stopped containers at once.
